title: Changing a Public Method Signature
hints: A public or protected method on a class that is not final is an override point: something outside the package may already override it, and PHP compares the two declarations when that subclass is loaded.

Adding a parameter to such a method is a signature change, an optional one included. The subclass that declares the old signature fatals as it is autoloaded — "Declaration of Sub::start() must be compatible with Base::start()" — and nothing in the class being edited names it.

hints.text: Nothing in a core checkout reports it. No core class has to override the method, so the unit, functional, coding-guidelines and static-analysis runs are all green on the change.

The core files such a change as breaking on the possibility of an override rather than on a demonstrated one. Its changelog entries name the affected installations as the extensions extending the method, and one that calls that set very unlikely files it as breaking anyway.

The exception is a member the core has taken out of its public API with @internal, which takes an Important entry instead of a Breaking one. An entry is still owed; only its type changes, and that is what lets such a change reach a release line.

So the target branch is decided here rather than at commit-message time. A maintained release line carries no breaking change, no deprecation and no feature, which leaves Important the only one of the four it takes — a fix owed to one cannot carry the signature change at all.

hints: Add rather than widen where the change has to reach a release line: a method of its own, or the state handed over on something the callee already receives — the core puts the calling ContentObjectRenderer on the request as the currentContentObject attribute instead of into a signature. Declaring the class or the method final first is no cheaper, because that is itself a breaking change with an entry of its own.

hints.text: Which entries decide each of those, and what the extension scanner can and cannot find, is typo3_rule_lookup(query "breaking change").
A change that moves no member at all is settled the other way round, on what it renders: typo3_hint_lookup with the id breaking-without-a-moved-member.

hints: A shipped TypeScript module has no compile-time consumer: no .d.ts stands below typo3/sysext and Build/tsconfig.json emits none, so a changed member type breaks no build outside the core. What a consumer reaches is the built JavaScript below Resources/Public/JavaScript, where protected is a word the build dropped, so the surface is every export and every member a module outside the core can call.

A moved or renamed export of a shipped module gets a Deprecation changelog entry with the :js: role and a deprecation notice in the browser console, as the core wrote when it moved markFieldAsChanged() out of @typo3/backend/form-engine-validation. A module marked @internal in its TypeScript owes none.

title: Whether a Change Is Breaking When No Member Moved
appliesTo: does this bugfix owe a changelog entry
hints: A change that moves no PHP member can still be breaking. The core defines the type as functionality that may break or affect third-party code, and affect is what carries a change in what an installation renders.

So the second test is what an installation renders, or is configured by, for content nobody edited. A changed frontend markup, a changed or removed default TypoScript setting, a changed shipped Fluid template and a removed configuration option each carry it.
The core files these as breaking routinely rather than as exceptions, and its changelog guide offers "Frontend output may change" as an example of what an Impact section says.
Important is not the smaller version of breaking. It is the last resort for a change none of the other three types describes, so what takes it is an addition that leaves existing output alone.

Where the effect is the same, the target branch decides between the two. Such a change is breaking on main, and on a maintained release line it takes an Important instead — that line takes a breaking entry only as a rare exemption for a very important fix.

So the type settles the backport rather than following it. A patch that changes what is rendered and names a maintained line in its Releases trailer is a contradiction to settle before the entry is written.
